name: Punta Cana International Airport
label: Punta Cana Airport
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Terminal B' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Terminal B (Arrival & Departure)' (way/335430650): middle (397 m across); moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/256151866: large area 'Punta Cana International Airport' (5014 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Famous for its palm-thatched roof terminals.

text.description:
Punta Cana International Airport has a look of its own. It was built with open-air terminals and roofs covered in palm fronds, and when it opened in December 1983 it became the first privately owned international airport in the world. It is now the busiest airport in the Dominican Republic, with more than 8.3 million passengers in 2022. Terminal B, opened in November 2014, is the fully enclosed, modern one, with jet bridges.

For photos, the best option is the outdoor terrace in Terminal B, near gates B25 and B26. It faces the taxiway, so aircraft roll past at close range with the gate area behind them. That gives you a travel-day picture with real movement in it, and it is easy to take with a phone.

The terrace is after security, so you need a boarding pass to reach it. It is not a street-level spot for the general public. A glass barrier runs along the front, and you may need to see over it. If you shoot close to the glass, reflections can be a nuisance, so hold the phone close to the glass and shade the screen with your hand. Take the photo while you wait for your flight, and follow any instructions from airport staff. Rules for photography around airports can change, so check the official airport site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The airport is in the Punta Cana area on the eastern side of the Dominican Republic. The terrace itself is inside Terminal B, after security.
text.directions_text: Reach the airport by road and head for the Terminal B departures area. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Once through security, walk to the gates around B25 and B26, where the outdoor terrace overlooks the taxiway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for aircraft passing close by, with the gate area in the frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for planes further along the taxiway. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole gate frontage; it makes aircraft look small and slightly stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (outdoor terrace near gates B25 and B26, facing the taxiway). Aircraft taxiing in front of the terrace at close range, with the terminal's gate area in the frame. The photo itself is not taken at the icon. The actual spot is the outdoor terrace inside Terminal B, after security, near gates B25 and B26, facing the taxiway. From there aircraft taxi in front of you at close range, with the terminal's gate area in the frame. Choose a spot along the terrace where the glass is clean and you can see clearly.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the taxiing aircraft on one of the lower third lines, leaving space in front of it to show it is moving. Include a bit of the gate area so the picture says 'airport'. Hold the phone close to the glass to cut reflections. Take a short burst or a Live Photo as the plane passes, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the aircraft to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not turn white and the plane keeps its detail. Keep your hands steady and take several shots, as planes keep moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Winter is the best time for this terrace, as the light is better. In summer the afternoon light comes from behind the aircraft and makes the photos backlit.

text.access_note: The Terminal B terrace is after security, so you need a boarding pass, and photography rules can change, so check the official airport site before you go.

name: Playa Blanca (Punta Cana)
label: Playa Blanca
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Playa Blanca' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W907574862 (Playa Blanca): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: White-sand beach at the Puntacana Resort.

text.description:
Playa Blanca is a beach with shallow turquoise water, and it is a good place for relaxed holiday photos. The corner people photograph most is in the shallow water, where swings are set out from the sand. Someone sitting on a swing with the turquoise sea behind them gives a 'floating over the ocean' look. It also suits a romantic couple shot. Two other pictures are worth making. One is the painted Playa Blanca sign in the foreground, with the glittering sea behind it. The other is a wide view down over the beach and coastline, taken from the cliff above the restaurant. That cliff has no separate name, so look for the best angle once you are there.

The beach is inside a gated resort area, so it is not a casual stop. The swings and the sign may be moved or taken away, so treat them as a bonus and not a certainty. If they are missing, the turquoise water and the line of the shore still make a good picture.

For the swing shot, let the person on the swing fill the lower half of the frame so the sea fills the rest. Take a few frames in a row, because swings move and eyes close. Before you wade out, wipe your lens with a dry cloth. Salt spray and sunscreen leave smears that look like haze in bright light.
text.geographic_location: Playa Blanca is on the coast of the Punta Cana area, inside the gated Puntacana/Cap Cana resort area. A restaurant is associated with the beach, and a cliff above the restaurant is described as a viewpoint.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this beach. Expect to stop at the main gate of the resort area and register with ID and vehicle details. Once on the beach, walk down to the water's edge, where the swings stand in the shallows. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the swing shot, so the person looks natural against the sea. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sign with the sea behind it. Try telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) from the sand to bring the swing and the water closer without wading out.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Photograph the person on the swing with the turquoise sea behind them. For the sign, stand a few steps back on the sand so the lettering is in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the swing on one third of the frame, leaving open sea beside it. Keep the horizon level. For the wide view, use panorama mode from the cliff above the restaurant. As an alternative to the swings, take the sign with the sea glittering behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the person or the sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sea stays blue and does not wash out. Use Live Photos or a quick burst on the swing so you can choose the best moment. Keep your phone dry near the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the sand. Midday sun can make the sea glare, so lower the exposure slider if you shoot then.

text.access_note: This beach is inside a gated resort area, where visitors register with ID and vehicle details at the main gate. Guides report an entrance fee or a restaurant voucher, but access conditions and any charges can change, so check before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Midday sun can cause glare on the sea.
Salt spray and sunscreen can smear a phone lens.
The swings and sign may be moved or removed, so they may not be there when you visit.

name: Hoyo Azul
label: Hoyo Azul
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hoyo Azul' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N3159381465 (Hoyo Azul): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Turquoise freshwater cenote at Scape Park.

text.description:
Hoyo Azul is a natural pool in the limestone, with water that looks strikingly turquoise when the sun reaches it. A cliff rises behind the pool and the jungle crowds in around the edges. That mix of bright water, pale rock and green leaves makes it easy to photograph, even with a phone. Visitors reach it inside Scape Park Punta Cana in Cap Cana, so it is part of a park day rather than a quick roadside stop.

The best views are from the wooden walkway and the stair platforms at the edge of the pool. These give you a safe, steady place to stand and look across the water to the cliff. Guides describe the colour of the water as the main attraction, so make it the centre of your picture and let the cliff and trees frame it. Your best shot is the turquoise pool with the cliff behind and the jungle around it.

The water is lovely in direct sun, but the surrounding rock and leaves can be dark and patchy. Take a few frames at different moments and compare them. If you want to shoot close to the water, some guides suggest a waterproof case for your phone. Inside the park there is also a suspension bridge on the forest path and a wooden staircase down to the water, which may be quieter spots for a second angle. Entry is by park ticket, and the park may restrict some equipment, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Hoyo Azul is inside Scape Park Punta Cana, in the Cap Cana area of Punta Cana. You reach it by walking through the park's forest paths.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve this spot, so head for Scape Park Punta Cana in Cap Cana. Once inside the park, follow the forest path to the cenote. The wooden walkway and stair platforms at the pool's edge are where you stand. Check the park's official site for entry details before you travel. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the pool, the cliff and the jungle frame into one shot from the platforms. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view across the water. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the cliff face or the colour of the water without leaning over the edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you look across the pool to the cliff, with the jungle framing the sides. The turquoise water is the part to build the picture around.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the waterline on a lower third line, with the cliff filling the upper part. Let the leaves and branches make a natural frame at the edges. A once-inside alternative is the suspension bridge on the forest path or the wooden staircase down to the water, which may be quieter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the turquoise stays rich and the highlights are not washed out. Keep a dry cloth handy to wipe the lens. If you go close to the water, use a waterproof case, as guides suggest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive, is the most common advice. Some guides prefer mid-morning to mid-afternoon (around 10:00 to 14:00), when direct sun lights the water and gives the bluest colour. If you can, try both.

text.access_note: Hoyo Azul is reached only inside Scape Park Punta Cana on a park ticket, and the park may restrict professional photo equipment and drones, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Hoyo Azul means 'Blue Hole' in Spanish and the feature is a natural cenote (limestone sinkhole pool).
The shaded rock and foliage around the pool can create strong contrast with the sunlit water.
Spray or damp air near the water can smudge a phone lens, so a dry cloth helps.
Lowering the exposure slider on bright water helps keep its colour from washing out.

notes: Clifftop golf course with ocean views.

text.description:
Corales Golf Course is part of the Puntacana Resort and Club in Punta Cana, in the La Altagracia province of the Dominican Republic. Tom Fazio designed it and it opened in 2010. It is known for holes that run right along the Caribbean shoreline, and for hosting the PGA Tour's Corales Puntacana Championship since 2018. The course will also host the golf event at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games.

For a phone photo, the best picture is the oceanfront 9th hole, a short par 3 whose green sits against the sea. Get low and frame the green in the foreground, with the waves breaking on the rocks directly behind it. The mix of mown grass, dark rock and moving water gives you a clear foreground, middle and background without any fuss. If you would rather have a simpler souvenir shot, the white lettering of the course sign works well, with the fairway, rocky coast and open sea behind it. The clubhouse may also offer an elevated view down over the 18th hole and the other greens beside the sea, so check it is open to visitors.

The holes are for players, so take your photos from the edges, stay out of the way and avoid slowing play. The sign and clubhouse are reached through the resort.
text.geographic_location: On the Punta Cana coast in La Altagracia, inside the private Puntacana Resort & Club, with the course running along the Caribbean shoreline.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is near. The course is inside the private Puntacana Resort & Club, so ask at the resort entrance or clubhouse how to get there. Check the official site before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the green, the rocks and the waves in one low frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the course sign with the sea behind it. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the waves breaking behind the green from the edge of the course.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you get a low angle of the 9th green with the Caribbean waves breaking on the rocks directly behind it. Stay on the edge of the hole and keep clear of players.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch and hold the phone low, just above the grass, so the green fills the foreground and the sea sits behind it. Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with a top third line so it stays level. For a different shot, the course sign works as a foreground with the fairway, rocky coast and sea behind it. The clubhouse may offer an elevated view down over the 18th hole and the other ocean-side greens, if it is open to visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the sea to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white spray keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as the waves change from one shot to the next. A Live Photo can catch the waves breaking.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water and avoids harsh midday glare. Avoid busy playing times so you stay out of the golfers' way.

text.access_note: The course is inside the private Puntacana Resort & Club and the holes are for players, so check the official site before you go and ask about photography and visitor access.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on the sea than midday light.
Gridlines help keep the horizon level in a phone photo.
The course is likely to be busiest with golfers at certain times of day, so photographing outside peak playing times is easier.

name: Cabeza de Toro
label: Cabeza de Toro Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Playa Cabeza de Toro' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W27579781 (Playa Cabeza de Toro): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Quiet palm-lined beach north of the airport.

text.description:
Playa Cabeza de Toro is a public beach with a calm, shallow bay of turquoise water. The coral rock outcrops at each end of the bay act as natural frame edges, and a palm-lined shore sits along the near side. Together they give you an easy, balanced beach picture without much effort. The name means 'bull's head'. That shape is best seen from above, so from the sand you are photographing the bay itself rather than the rock profile.

The phone icon on the map is on the beach itself. Walk down to the waterline at either end of the bay, close to the coral outcrops. From there you can put one outcrop in the corner of the frame, let the bay open out behind it, and keep a few palms in the foreground. The water is calm and shallow, so the surface stays smooth and the colours look clean on a phone screen.

If you want a different picture, there is a second beach, Cabeza de Toro Private Beach, which has a swing and a bamboo pier. It is for resort guests only, so it is not a free public viewpoint. Check the rules before planning around it.

Go early. About two hours after sunrise the water is glassy and the light is soft. Keep your phone dry and clean the lens with a soft cloth before you shoot, as sea spray leaves a haze.
text.geographic_location: Playa Cabeza de Toro is a beach on the Punta Cana coast in the Dominican Republic. The rock outcrops mark both ends of its bay.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops serve this beach, so check local options for getting there. The phone icon on the map is on the beach itself, so once you reach the sand you are already at the spot. Walk along the waterline to either end of the bay to reach the coral outcrops. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole bay, an outcrop and the palms in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the texture of the coral rock or a single palm against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Playa Cabeza de Toro at the waterline at either end of the bay, near the coral rock outcrops. From there the photo shows the turquoise bay framed between the outcrops, with the palm-lined shore in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line, not in the middle. Keep an outcrop in one corner and the palms along the near edge so the bay sits between them. If you also visit Cabeza de Toro Private Beach as an alternative, which is for resort guests only, its swing and bamboo pier make a staged scene against the palms and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the turquoise stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone level, or the horizon will tilt. Live Photos can catch gentle ripples if you stand still for a moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, about two hours after sunrise, when the water is glassy and the light is soft.

text.access_note: Playa Cabeza de Toro is a public beach, but access rules can change, and the private beach is for resort guests only, so check current access rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Playa Cabeza de Toro is on the Punta Cana coast in the Dominican Republic.
Sea spray can leave a haze on a phone lens, so wiping it with a soft cloth helps.

text.description:
Cap Cana is a large private resort and residential district on the Dominican Republic's eastern coast, and it is the second stop on this map. It covers roughly 123 square kilometres, so no single frame shows all of it. Most visitors photograph it in pieces: the beach, the marina, the golf coast and the hotels.

For this spot the best place to start is Playa Juanillo. The water here is calm and glassy, which suits soft reflections and relaxed portraits, and the resort shoreline makes a tidy backdrop. Catamarans anchored offshore give you something to pick out with a zoom.

A few facts help set the scene. Building began in the early 2000s. Punta Espada Golf Club, designed by Jack Nicklaus, opened in November 2006, and the first phase of Marina Cap Cana followed in 2007. The marina is the classic place for yacht-and-waterfront pictures, so if you have time, make it a second stop.

For a wider coastal view, the Farallon high point is another option, though it is described as a steep climb.

On your phone, keep the shot simple. Put the waterline on a gridline, tap the sea or the boats to set focus, and lower the exposure slightly if the sky is bright. Wipe the lens first, as sea air and sunscreen smear it easily.
text.geographic_location: Cap Cana is a gated resort district on the eastern coast of La Altagracia Province, in the Punta Cana area. Juanillo Beach is one of its coastal areas, and the marina and golf coast lie elsewhere within the district.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so you will need to arrange your own way to the Cap Cana area on the eastern coast. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the calm water and shoreline. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more beach and sky in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the catamarans anchored offshore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (shoreline of the Juanillo beach, looking back toward the Cap Cana coast). Calm, glassy water and the resort shoreline, with catamarans anchored offshore that can be framed with a zoom lens. You will see calm, glassy water and the resort shoreline, with catamarans anchored offshore.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the waterline on the lower third so the glassy water fills the frame. Use the telephoto to isolate a catamaran against the shoreline. For portraits, switch to portrait mode and keep your subject a little way from the water's edge. If you also visit Marina Cap Cana, frame the moored yachts with the waterfront buildings behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the boats to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the water stays smooth. Try a Live Photo to catch gentle movement on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a quieter beach. Calm water is what makes the reflections work, so choose a still day if you can.

text.access_note: Cap Cana is a gated resort district, so some areas may need a visitor pass or be restricted, and the Juanillo beach gate is only described as public during the day; check the official site before you go.

text.description: Puntacana Resort & Club is a large resort and residential community on the eastern tip of the Dominican Republic. For photos, Playa Blanca, the beach on the ocean side of the resort, is the scene to aim for. Views of Playa Blanca show white sand and turquoise water in the foreground, with the resort's buildings and palm trees behind. Guides describe Playa Blanca as the resort's main public beach, with some of the clearest water in Punta Cana. It is a natural spot for a resort-backdrop picture. The Westin Puntacana Resort & Club stands in this Playa Blanca area, and a beachside restaurant sits on the sand. The resort was founded in 1969 by Frank Rainieri and Theodore Kheel, who began with a 40-guest hotel called the Punta Cana Club on a stretch of jungle and beach. It has since grown to about 15,000 acres. For a good phone photo, keep the horizon or waterline level with the gridlines and let any sand or shoreline lead the eye towards the palms and buildings. Add a few people or a lounger for scale. Take a few frames at different heights, because a low phone angle makes sand look more dramatic. Wipe the lens first, as sea air leaves a film on it.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (beach on the ocean side of the resort, shooting back toward the property). If you want a second view, the beach in front of the Westin has a pier and cabanas, with lounge chairs and palms framing the scene, but that beach may be for guests only.

notes: Easternmost point of the island, with a lighthouse.

text.description:
Cape Engaño is the easternmost point of the island of Hispaniola, where the Dominican Republic meets the open Atlantic. The Faro de Cabo Engaño, a red-and-white striped lighthouse, is the obvious subject here. It photographs well because the bold stripes stand out against the sky and sea, and the coast behind gives you a sense of how far out on the edge of the island you are. Walking up to the base of the tower lets you shoot upwards from ground level with the coastline behind.

The cape has a long history. In 1502, a large Spanish fleet of 30 to 32 ships, carrying treasure, colonists and others bound for Spain, was caught in a violent storm somewhere close to the cape. Most of the ships were lost, and the cape is still known for dangerous reefs offshore. Punta Cana International Airport lies a little to the south.

Getting here takes effort. Guides describe the last 6 to 8 km as sandy and rutted, and the road may be impassable after heavy rain. Check the lighthouse's current state before you set out. Early morning or late afternoon gives the softest light. Bring water and sun protection, because the area is exposed.
text.geographic_location: Cape Engaño is at the easternmost point of Hispaniola, on the Atlantic coast. Punta Cana International Airport lies slightly to the south of it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed nearby, so start from the airport and head north towards the cape. The cape is at the eastern tip of the island. Go by 4x4, buggy or guided ATV tour, as guides advise this for the sandy, rutted last 6 to 8 km. Check the road conditions first, especially after heavy rain. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the foot of the tower to capture the full height of the stripes with sky and coastline. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the tower with the Atlantic behind. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the lighthouse, walking up to the tower). The red-and-white lighthouse tower in the foreground, with the Atlantic coastline behind it, framed from ground level at its base. For a closer view, you can also walk up to the base of the tower, where the red-and-white tower stands in the foreground with the Atlantic coastline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch and tilt the phone upwards so the tower rises from the bottom of the frame, with the coastline in the background. Turn on gridlines and keep the tower upright against a vertical line. For a different shot, step back and frame the lighthouse as a silhouette against a pink-orange dawn sky over the sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the white stripes don't wash out. At dawn, try night mode only if the light is very dim, and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, for soft golden light.

text.access_note: Access is by a rough sandy track and the lighthouse's current state is uncertain, so check current conditions with a local operator before you go.
